notes.definition: Animal and plant cells are eukaryotic cells made up of sub-cellular structures, each with a specific function. Most animal cells have a nucleus, cytoplasm, cell membrane, mitochondria and ribosomes; plant cells also often have chloroplasts and a permanent vacuole, and plant and algal cells have a cellulose cell wall.
explanation: Cells contain smaller parts called sub-cellular structures. Most animal cells have five: a nucleus, cytoplasm, a cell membrane, mitochondria and ribosomes. Each one has a job. The nucleus contains genetic material that controls the activities of the cell. The cytoplasm is a gel-like substance where most of the chemical reactions happen; it contains enzymes that control these reactions. The cell membrane controls the movement of substances into and out of the cell.

Mitochondria are where the reactions of aerobic respiration take place. Aerobic respiration releases the energy that the cell needs, so cells that use a lot of energy, such as muscle cells, contain many mitochondria. Ribosomes are tiny structures where protein synthesis happens: amino acids are joined together to make proteins such as enzymes. Ribosomes are so small that they can only be seen with an electron microscope.

Plant cells have all the structures found in animal cells, plus some extra ones. Many plant cells have chloroplasts, which contain the green pigment chlorophyll. Chloroplasts absorb light, and photosynthesis takes place inside them. Not all plant cells have chloroplasts: cells in roots, which receive no light, have none. Plant cells also have a permanent vacuole filled with cell sap, a solution of sugars and salts in water, which helps keep the cell firm.

Plant cells and algal cells have a cell wall made of cellulose outside the cell membrane. The cell wall strengthens the cell and supports it, so it keeps its shape. The cell wall is freely permeable, so it does not control what enters the cell: that is the job of the cell membrane. Bacterial cells also have a cell wall, but it is not made of cellulose. Bacteria may also contain plasmids, small rings of DNA that carry extra genes.

Biologists often need to judge the relative size or area of sub-cellular structures. Estimation is useful when an exact measurement is not needed, when there is no scale available, or to quickly check that a calculated answer is sensible. For example, if a cell is 40 μm across and its nucleus looks about a quarter of the width of the cell, the nucleus is roughly 10 μm across. The area of a cell can be estimated by treating it as a simple shape such as a rectangle.
keyFacts: Nucleus: contains genetic material that controls the activities of the cell.
Cytoplasm: gel-like substance where most chemical reactions happen; contains enzymes that control these reactions.
Cell membrane: controls the movement of substances into and out of the cell.
Mitochondria: where aerobic respiration takes place, releasing energy.
Ribosomes: where protein synthesis takes place.
Chloroplasts: where photosynthesis takes place; they contain chlorophyll, which absorbs light.
Cell wall: made of cellulose in plant and algal cells; strengthens the cell.
Most animal cells have a nucleus, cytoplasm, cell membrane, mitochondria and ribosomes.
Plant cells often have chloroplasts and a permanent vacuole, and always have a cellulose cell wall.

keyTerms.definition: A part inside a cell that has a specific function, such as the nucleus or a mitochondrion.
The structure that contains the genetic material, which controls the activities of the cell.
The gel-like substance inside the cell membrane where most chemical reactions take place, controlled by enzymes.
A sub-cellular structure where aerobic respiration takes place (plural: mitochondria).
A very small sub-cellular structure where protein synthesis takes place.
A sub-cellular structure in some plant and algal cells that contains chlorophyll and is the site of photosynthesis.
A large space in a plant cell filled with cell sap.
The substance that plant and algal cell walls are made of. It strengthens the cell.
Using an approximate value, such as comparing a structure to the size of the whole cell, to judge size or area quickly.

workedExamples.title: Estimating the size of a sub-cellular structure
workedExamples.question: An animal cell is 40 μm across. In a photograph, its nucleus looks about one quarter of the width of the cell. Estimate the diameter of the nucleus.
steps: The nucleus is about 1/4 of the cell width.

workedExamples.title: Estimating the area of a cell and a vacuole
workedExamples.question: A plant cell is roughly rectangular, 60 μm long and 20 μm wide. Its permanent vacuole fills about three quarters of the cell. Estimate the area of the vacuole.
steps: Treat the cell as a rectangle: area = length × width = 60 μm × 20 μm = 1200 μm².
The vacuole fills about 3/4 of the cell: 1200 × 0.75 = 900 μm².

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think that all plant cells have chloroplasts.
misconceptions.right: In fact only plant cells that receive light usually have chloroplasts. Root hair cells and onion bulb cells, for example, have none.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the cell wall controls what enters and leaves a plant cell.
misconceptions.right: In fact the cell wall is freely permeable and its job is to strengthen the cell. The cell membrane controls the movement of substances into and out of the cell.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think that plant cells do not respire because they photosynthesise.
misconceptions.right: In fact plant cells have mitochondria and carry out respiration all the time, day and night.
In fact energy cannot be made. Mitochondria are where aerobic respiration takes place, which releases energy from glucose.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think every animal cell has a nucleus.
misconceptions.right: In fact 'most' animal cells have a nucleus. Mature red blood cells, for example, have no nucleus.

realWorld: Cellulose from plant cell walls is used to make paper and cotton fabric, and in our diet it acts as fibre.
Many poisons, such as cyanide, kill by stopping the reactions in mitochondria, so cells can no longer release energy by aerobic respiration.
Some antibiotics work by targeting bacterial ribosomes, which differ slightly from human ribosomes, so they stop bacteria making proteins without harming our cells.
examTips: Learn the exact function wording: 'the cell membrane controls the movement of substances in and out of the cell'. Avoid vague answers like 'protects the cell'.
Say 'mitochondria are where aerobic respiration takes place', not 'mitochondria make energy'. Energy is released, never made.
If asked for structures in plant cells but not animal cells, give cell wall, chloroplasts and permanent vacuole. Do not give nucleus, cytoplasm or mitochondria.
When asked to estimate, show the simple comparison you used, for example 'the nucleus is about one quarter of the cell width, so 40 ÷ 4 = 10 μm'.

In 'explain' questions about a cell with many mitochondria or ribosomes, link the structure to the process: more mitochondria means more respiration and more energy released; more ribosomes means more protein made.
summary: Animal cells: nucleus, cytoplasm, cell membrane, mitochondria, ribosomes.
Plant cells also have a cellulose cell wall, a permanent vacuole and often chloroplasts.
Nucleus controls the cell; cytoplasm is where most reactions happen.
Cell membrane controls movement of substances in and out.
Mitochondria: aerobic respiration. Ribosomes: protein synthesis. Chloroplasts: photosynthesis.
Estimation is used to judge the relative size or area of sub-cellular structures.

flashcards.back: Contains genetic material that controls the activities of the cell.

flashcards.front: What is in the permanent vacuole?
What are plant cell walls made of, and what do they do?
Name the five structures found in most animal cells.
flashcards.back: Nucleus, cytoplasm, cell membrane, mitochondria, ribosomes.

flashcards.front: Name three structures plant cells have that animal cells do not.
Why do root cells have no chloroplasts?
flashcards.back: They are underground, so receive no light for photosynthesis.

flashcards.front: When is estimation useful in cell biology?
flashcards.back: To judge relative size or area quickly, when exact measurement is not needed or possible, or to check a calculated answer.

questions.question: In which sub-cellular structure does aerobic respiration take place?
markScheme: 1 mark: mitochondrion
questions.explanation: Mitochondria are the site of aerobic respiration. Ribosomes make proteins, the nucleus holds genetic material and the cell membrane controls what enters and leaves.

questions.question: Which structure controls the movement of substances into and out of a cell?
markScheme: 1 mark: cell membrane
questions.explanation: The cell membrane controls what passes in and out. The cell wall is freely permeable and only strengthens the cell, so it is a common wrong answer.

questions.question: Where does protein synthesis take place?
markScheme: 1 mark: ribosomes
questions.explanation: Ribosomes join amino acids together to make proteins. Mitochondria release energy by respiration, and chloroplasts carry out photosynthesis.

questions.question: Which structure is found in plant cells but not in animal cells?
markScheme: 1 mark: chloroplast
questions.explanation: Chloroplasts are found only in some plant and algal cells. Ribosomes, mitochondria and cell membranes are found in both animal and plant cells.

questions.question: What substance are plant cell walls made of?
markScheme: 1 mark: cellulose
questions.explanation: Plant and algal cell walls are made of cellulose, which strengthens the cell. Starch is a storage carbohydrate, glycogen is stored in animal cells, and chlorophyll is the green pigment in chloroplasts.

questions.question: Which best describes the role of the cytoplasm?
options: It is where photosynthesis takes place
It stores the genetic information of the cell
It is where most of the cell's chemical reactions take place, controlled by enzymes
It makes cellulose to build the cell wall and nothing else
markScheme: 1 mark: it is where most of the cell's chemical reactions take place, controlled by enzymes
questions.explanation: The cytoplasm is a gel-like substance containing enzymes that control most chemical reactions. Photosynthesis happens in chloroplasts and genetic information is in the nucleus.

questions.question: A cell from a plant root has a nucleus, a cell wall and a permanent vacuole, but no chloroplasts. What is the best explanation for the lack of chloroplasts?
options: Root cells are underground and receive no light, so they cannot photosynthesise
The cell must be an animal cell
Chloroplasts are only found in algae
The cell wall stops chloroplasts forming
markScheme: 1 mark: root cells are underground and receive no light, so they cannot photosynthesise
questions.explanation: Chloroplasts are only useful where there is light for photosynthesis. The cell wall and permanent vacuole show it is a plant cell, not an animal cell.

questions.question: Which list contains ONLY structures found in both animal and plant cells?
options: Cell wall, permanent vacuole, chloroplasts, cytoplasm
markScheme: 1 mark: nucleus, cell membrane, mitochondria, ribosomes
questions.explanation: Animal and plant cells share a nucleus, cytoplasm, cell membrane, mitochondria and ribosomes. Cell walls, chloroplasts and permanent vacuoles are only in plant cells, and plasmids are found in bacteria.

questions.question: Muscle cells contain many more mitochondria than skin cells. What is the best explanation?
options: Muscle cells make more proteins in their mitochondria
Muscle cells need to carry out photosynthesis
Muscle cells need more energy, which is released by aerobic respiration in mitochondria
Mitochondria strengthen the muscle cell so it can contract
markScheme: 1 mark: muscle cells need more energy, which is released by aerobic respiration in mitochondria
questions.explanation: Contraction needs a lot of energy. More mitochondria means more aerobic respiration and more energy released. Proteins are made on ribosomes, not in mitochondria, and animal cells do not photosynthesise.

questions.question: A cell has a nucleus, a cellulose cell wall and a large permanent vacuole, but no chloroplasts. Which cell is it most likely to be?
markScheme: 1 mark: onion epidermis cell
questions.explanation: The cellulose wall and permanent vacuole show a plant cell, and the lack of chloroplasts fits an onion bulb cell, which grows without light. Bacteria have no nucleus, liver cells have no cell wall, and palisade cells are packed with chloroplasts.

questions.question: An animal cell is 10 μm long. A mitochondrion inside it is about one fifth of the length of the cell. Estimate the length of the mitochondrion.
markScheme: 1 mark: 2 μm
questions.explanation: One fifth of 10 μm is 10 ÷ 5 = 2 μm. This fits with mitochondria typically being about 1 to 2 μm long.

questions.question: A cheek cell is 40 μm across. In a photograph, its nucleus appears to be about one quarter of the width of the cell. Estimate the diameter of the nucleus.
markScheme: 1 mark: 10 μm
questions.explanation: 40 μm ÷ 4 = 10 μm. Estimation uses the known size of the whole cell to judge the relative size of a structure inside it.

questions.question: A plant cell is approximately rectangular, 60 μm long and 20 μm wide. Estimate the area of the cell.
markScheme: 1 mark: area = 60 × 20
1 mark: 1200 μm²
questions.explanation: Treat the cell as a rectangle: area = length × width = 60 × 20 = 1200 μm². The unit is squared because it is an area.

questions.question: A plant cell is roughly rectangular, 80 μm long and 30 μm wide. Its permanent vacuole takes up about 70% of the area of the cell. Estimate the area of the vacuole.
markScheme: 1 mark: area of cell = 80 × 30 = 2400 μm²
1 mark: 2400 × 0.7 = 1680 μm² (accept about 1700 μm²)
questions.explanation: Cell area = 80 × 30 = 2400 μm². 70% of 2400 = 0.7 × 2400 = 1680 μm². Because this is an estimate, an answer of about 1700 μm² is acceptable.

questions.question: A student counts an average of 15 chloroplasts per palisade cell. A small piece of leaf contains about 400 palisade cells. Estimate the number of chloroplasts in the palisade cells of this piece of leaf.
markScheme: 1 mark: 6000
questions.explanation: Multiply the average per cell by the number of cells: 15 × 400 = 6000 chloroplasts. Using a mean from a sample of cells is a sensible way to estimate a total that would be impractical to count.

questions.question: State the function of the nucleus.
acceptedAnswers: controls the activities of the cell
markScheme: 1 mark: contains genetic material which controls the activities of the cell
questions.explanation: The nucleus contains the genetic material (DNA) which controls what the cell does, including which proteins it makes.

questions.question: Name the green substance in chloroplasts that absorbs light.
markScheme: 1 mark: chlorophyll
questions.explanation: Chlorophyll is the green pigment inside chloroplasts. It absorbs light energy for photosynthesis. Do not confuse it with chloroplast, which is the structure.

questions.question: Name two structures found in plant cells that are not found in animal cells.
markScheme: 1 mark each for any two from: cell wall; chloroplasts; permanent vacuole
questions.explanation: Plant cells have a cellulose cell wall, a permanent vacuole and often chloroplasts. Animal cells have none of these.

questions.question: Describe the cell wall of a plant cell. Include what it is made of and its function.
markScheme: 1 mark: made of cellulose
1 mark: strengthens / supports the cell
questions.explanation: Plant cell walls are made of cellulose and strengthen the cell, helping it keep its shape. The wall does not control what enters the cell.

questions.question: Describe the permanent vacuole of a plant cell.
markScheme: 1 mark: (large) space / structure filled with cell sap
1 mark: cell sap is a solution of sugars and salts / helps keep the cell firm
questions.explanation: The permanent vacuole is a large space in the cytoplasm filled with cell sap, a solution of sugars and salts in water. When it is full of water it presses outwards and keeps the cell firm.

questions.question: Explain why the cytoplasm is important to a cell.
acceptedAnswers: most chemical reactions take place there
markScheme: 1 mark: it is where most of the chemical reactions in the cell take place
1 mark: it contains enzymes that control these reactions
questions.explanation: The cytoplasm is the site of most chemical reactions in the cell. The enzymes it contains control the rate of these reactions.

questions.question: Cells in the pancreas make large amounts of digestive enzymes. Suggest which sub-cellular structure these cells contain in large numbers. Explain your answer.
markScheme: 1 mark: ribosomes
1 mark: enzymes are proteins and ribosomes are where protein synthesis takes place
questions.explanation: Enzymes are proteins, and proteins are made on ribosomes. A cell making lots of enzyme therefore needs many ribosomes. (It would also need many mitochondria to release energy for this, which is a creditworthy extra point.)

questions.question:
A student looks at a micrograph of a cell with no scale bar. She knows the cell is about 30 μm long.
Explain how and why she could use estimation to judge the size of the nucleus.
acceptedAnswers: compare to the size of the cell
markScheme: 1 mark: compare the nucleus with the whole cell, e.g. judge what fraction of the cell length it is
1 mark: multiply that fraction by 30 μm (e.g. one third gives 10 μm)
1 mark: estimation is useful because there is no scale bar / exact measurement is not possible or not needed / to check a calculated answer is sensible
questions.explanation: Without a scale bar, the known cell length acts as a reference. If the nucleus spans about a third of the cell, it is roughly 30 ÷ 3 = 10 μm. Estimation gives a quick, sensible value when a precise measurement is not needed or not possible.

questions.question: State where photosynthesis takes place in a plant cell.
markScheme: 1 mark: chloroplast(s)
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis takes place in chloroplasts, which contain chlorophyll to absorb light.

questions.question: Bacterial cells may contain plasmids. Describe what a plasmid is and what it contains.
markScheme: 1 mark: a small ring / loop of DNA (separate from the main DNA)
1 mark: carries (extra) genes, e.g. for antibiotic resistance
questions.explanation: Plasmids are small rings of DNA in the cytoplasm of bacteria. They carry extra genes, such as genes that make the bacterium resistant to an antibiotic.

questions.question: Compare the structure of a typical animal cell with a typical leaf cell. Explain how the sub-cellular structures in each cell are related to their functions.
markScheme: Indicative content:
both have a nucleus containing genetic material that controls the cell
both have cytoplasm, where most reactions happen, controlled by enzymes
both have a cell membrane that controls movement of substances in and out
both have mitochondria for aerobic respiration, releasing energy
both have ribosomes for protein synthesis
only the leaf cell has a cellulose cell wall, which strengthens the cell
only the leaf cell has a permanent vacuole containing cell sap
only the leaf cell has chloroplasts, containing chlorophyll to absorb light for photosynthesis
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): clear comparison of shared and different structures, with the function of most structures correctly explained.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): several structures correctly identified as shared or different, with some functions given.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): a few structures named with little comparison or few functions.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: Top answers group the five shared structures with their functions, then explain the three extra plant structures. Linking each structure to what it does, such as chloroplasts absorbing light for photosynthesis, is what lifts an answer to Level 3.

questions.question:
A student looks at a cell from an onion bulb and a cell from the lining of her cheek using a light microscope.
Describe the differences she would expect to see between the two cells, and explain why the onion cell has no chloroplasts.
markScheme: Indicative content:
onion cell has a cell wall; cheek cell does not
onion cell has a (large) permanent vacuole; cheek cell does not
onion cell has a regular, box-like shape; cheek cell is irregular / rounded
both have a nucleus, cytoplasm and cell membrane
onion bulb grows underground / receives no light
so no photosynthesis takes place and chloroplasts are not needed
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): at least two correct differences plus a clear explanation linking lack of light to lack of chloroplasts.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): one difference or a simple explanation.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: The onion cell has a cellulose wall and a permanent vacuole, giving it a regular shape, while the cheek cell has neither. Onion bulb cells grow without light, so they cannot photosynthesise and do not need chloroplasts. Ribosomes are too small to see with a light microscope, so they would not be listed as visible differences.
